questions.q: State the valency of magnesium (atomic number 12) and explain how you determined it using its position in the Modern Periodic Table.
questions.a: Magnesium (Z=12) has electron configuration 2,8,2. It is in Group 2, Period 3. Valency = 2 (loses 2 electrons to achieve stable octet). A wrong answer like "valency = 12" reveals confusion between atomic number and valence electrons. Writing "valency = 6" (group number 16 style) shows misunderstanding that valency for metals = group number, not (8 - group number).

questions.q: Explain why atomic size decreases from sodium (Na) to chlorine (Cl) in Period 3, even though the number of electrons increases.
questions.a: Across Period 3, protons increase (11→17) while electrons add to the same M-shell (n=3). Effective nuclear charge increases, pulling the valence shell closer. No new shell is added. A student who says "size increases because more electrons" ignores nuclear charge dominance. Saying "shielding increases" is wrong — shielding by same-shell electrons is minimal.

questions.q: Element X is in Group 14, Period 3. Element Y is in Group 14, Period 4. Predict which has larger atomic size and by approximately how many picometers (pm), given that each new shell adds ~100-150 pm.
questions.a: X = Silicon (Si), Y = Germanium (Ge). Y is larger. Down Group 14, a new shell (N-shell) adds. Size increase ≈ 100-150 pm. Typical values: Si ~111 pm, Ge ~122 pm (covalent radii). Difference ~11 pm — smaller than 100 pm because d-electrons in Ge provide poor shielding. A student answering "X is larger" reverses the trend. Saying "difference is 100 pm exactly" ignores transition metal contraction effect.

questions.q: Compare the valency and atomic size trends for Group 1 (alkali metals) and Group 17 (halogens). Why do both groups show constant valency down the group but opposite reactivity trends?
questions.a: Group 1: Valency = 1 (loses 1 e⁻), size increases down group, reactivity increases (easier to lose e⁻). Group 17: Valency = 1 (gains 1 e⁻), size increases down group, reactivity decreases (harder to gain e⁻ due to lower effective nuclear charge on valence shell). Both have constant valence electrons (1 and 7). A student saying "both become more reactive" confuses metal vs non-metal reactivity. Saying "valency changes" ignores same-group valence electron count.

questions.q: A student claims: "Argon (Ar) has valency 8 because it has 8 valence electrons." Evaluate this statement and correct it using the concept of stable octet.
questions.a: Incorrect. Argon (Z=18, config 2,8,8) has 8 valence electrons but valency = 0. Valency is combining capacity — Ar has complete octet, does not lose, gain, or share electrons under normal conditions. The student confuses "valence electron count" with "valency". For noble gases, valency = 0 (except Xe, Kr under extreme conditions). Writing "valency = 8" would lose full marks in CBSE.

questions.q: Design a simple activity using the Modern Periodic Table to demonstrate that atomic size decreases across Period 2 but the rate of decrease is not uniform. What data would you plot and what pattern would you expect?
questions.a: Plot atomic radius (pm) vs atomic number for Li (152), Be (112), B (85), C (77), N (75), O (73), F (71), Ne (71) — covalent/van der Waals radii. Expect steep drop Li→Be (new p-subshell, poor shielding), then gradual decrease. Non-uniformity: biggest jump at Li→Be (s→p transition), then smaller steps. A student plotting "smooth curve" misses subshell effects. Using metallic radii for all gives wrong trend for non-metals.

questions.q: Fill in the blank: Valency is the combining capacity of an element ______ by the number of electrons in its outermost shell (valence electrons), while atomic size (atomic radius) is the distance from the nucleus to the outermost electron shell.
Fill in the blank: Start by showing a Class 10 student two familiar objects: a lithium battery (small, light) and a potassium ______ bag (larger atoms, more reactive).
What is Valency? State the definition given in this lesson.
questions.a: Valency is the combining capacity of an element determined by the number of electrons in its outermost shell (valence electrons), while atomic size (atomic radius) is the distance from the nucleus to the outermost electron shell.

questions.q: Fill in the blank: Then introduce the Modern Periodic Table: move left-to-right across Period ______ (Li to Ne) — nuclear charge increases, electrons add to same shell, size shrinks.
What common mix-up does this lesson flag about Valency?
questions.a: Students write "valency = group number for all elements" — e.g., oxygen (Group 16) valency = 6.

questions.q: What must you be able to do to master this topic?
questions.a: The student can predict the valency and relative atomic size of any element given its position in the Modern Periodic Table, explain the underlying reasons using nuclear charge and shielding effect, and solve CBSE board exam questions that combine these trends with chemical reactivity predictions.
